prompt: Why is it safe to reuse a stored KV prefix for a different request?

options.A: The server re-checks every value against the new request
options.B: It isn't fully safe; small errors are accepted for speed
options.C: Keys and values at position i depend only on tokens 1…i (the causal mask), so an identical prefix always gives identical KV
options.D: KV values are the same for every prompt

prompt: When would the cost gap between output and input tokens shrink? Pick all that apply.

options.A: Quantized weights, so each tick reads fewer bytes
options.B: Higher temperature
options.C: Smaller KV caches (shorter contexts, fewer KV heads), so more users fit in a batch
options.D: Longer contexts per request
options.E: Larger decode batches, so each weight read is shared by more users

prompt: Run those 6.3 × 10²⁴ operations on 8,192 GPUs at 989 trillion operations per second each, with 40% utilization. How many days?
Training runs all positions in parallel; generation runs one at a time. Why do the two compute the same thing?

options.A: The causal mask makes each position see only itself and earlier positions, exactly what it sees during generation
options.B: They don't; models are adjusted after training to match
options.C: Both use the same temperature
options.D: Generation retrains the model after each token

prompt: You ask a base model (pre-training only) “What is a river bank?” What is it most likely to do?

options.A: Return an error
options.B: Answer politely like a chat assistant
options.C: Refuse, because it has no instructions
options.D: Continue the text as a document would, perhaps with more quiz questions, rather than answer

prompt: On a cache hit for that 3,000-token prefix, what improves? Pick all that apply.

options.A: The answer gets more accurate
options.B: TPOT: each output token gets much faster
options.C: TTFT: only the new tokens need prefill
options.D: Input cost: providers bill cached input tokens at a discount

prompt: What would the model learn if you trained without the causal mask?

options.A: Nothing: training would crash
options.B: To copy the next token from the input, since it could see it; at generation time that token doesn't exist yet, so the trick fails
options.C: To generate whole sentences at once
options.D: Exactly the same thing, only slower

prompt: TTFT is 0.3 s and TPOT is 25 ms. How many seconds until a 401-token answer has fully arrived?
Training compute ≈ 6 × parameters × tokens. A 70B model on 15 trillion tokens. How many operations, in units of 10²⁴?
Why does pre-training need no human labels?

options.A: The text supplies the answer: the right label at each position is simply the next token
options.B: It does need labels; they are crowdsourced
options.C: Labels are added later, during fine-tuning
options.D: A smaller model labels the text first

prompt: An app sends a 3,000-token system prompt plus a short user message. How should it order the prompt to keep prompt-cache hits?

options.A: Fixed content first (system prompt, tools, examples), changing content (user message, timestamps) last
options.B: Put a timestamp at the top so the cache knows the prompt's age
options.C: Order doesn't matter; the cache matches any shared text
options.D: User message first so it gets the most attention

prompt: Which backend pattern is decode batching most like?

options.A: A CDN edge cache
options.B: A circuit breaker
options.C: Group commit: many transactions share one disk flush, so each waits slightly longer but total throughput rises
options.D: Read replicas

prompt: Loss = −ln p(correct token). The model gives the correct token 50%. What is the loss?
Which backend pattern is prompt caching most like?

options.A: A message queue
options.B: Database sharding
options.C: A write-through cache in front of a database
options.D: A content-addressed cache with a TTL: hash the prefix blocks, look them up, expire entries after minutes

prompt: Prefill floor: 2 operations per parameter per token. A 70B model on GPUs delivering 1,978 trillion operations per second in total. Minimum TTFT for a 2,000-token prompt, in milliseconds?
Same formula, but the model gives the correct token only 1%. What is the loss?
Llama 2 used about 27,540 written SFT examples versus about 2 trillion pre-training tokens. What does that say?

options.A: SFT examples are worth more than pre-training tokens for learning facts
options.B: SFT replaces most of what pre-training learned
options.C: Knowledge comes from pre-training; a small, high-quality post-training set mainly shapes behavior and format
options.D: Pre-training is mostly wasted

prompt: Why use −ln p instead of 1 − p as the loss?

options.A: 1 − p can be negative
options.B: There is no difference in what the model learns
options.C: −ln p is cheaper to compute
options.D: −ln p punishes confident wrong answers without limit (p → 0 gives loss → ∞), while 1 − p caps the penalty at 1

prompt: Which levers lower cost per million tokens? Pick all that apply.

options.A: More tokens per second while busy (batching, quantization, better kernels)
options.B: A bigger vocabulary
options.C: Lower temperature
options.D: A higher busy share of each paid hour (traffic, autoscaling, sharing GPUs across models)

prompt: Which backend idea is the causal mask most like?

options.A: A dead-letter queue
options.B: A load balancer
options.C: A snapshot read: each transaction sees only what was committed before it, never later writes
options.D: Rate limiting

prompt: Which are real differences between training and serving infrastructure? Pick all that apply.

options.A: Training uses a KV cache to skip recomputation
options.B: One failed GPU stalls a whole synchronized training job, so teams checkpoint often
options.C: Training needs several times the memory per parameter (gradients and optimizer state)
options.D: Training GPUs must exchange gradients every step, so the network and stragglers matter as much as the chips
options.E: Serving updates the weights after every request

prompt: Why does an output token cost more GPU time than an input token?

options.A: Output tokens are longer than input tokens
options.B: Input tokens are processed together in prefill, with the GPU's math fully busy; each output step reads all the weights and caches to emit just one token per user
options.C: Providers charge more for output to discourage long answers; GPU time is the same
options.D: Output tokens go through more layers

prompt: SFT scores only the answer tokens (weight 0 on the template and prompt). What would go wrong if it scored the prompt too?

options.A: The causal mask would stop working
options.B: The model would forget the vocabulary
options.C: Training effort would go into predicting user messages, so the model learns to write prompts as well as answers
options.D: Nothing; it only costs a little more compute

prompt: You raise the decode batch from 1 to 64. What happens?

options.A: Each user's TPOT stays exactly the same until compute runs out
options.B: Total tokens per second rises a lot; each user's TPOT rises a little; KV memory eventually caps how many users fit
options.C: Both throughput and each user's TPOT get better
options.D: Throughput stays the same; each user gets slower

prompt: Two GPUs at $4 per GPU-hour produce 1,000 output tokens per second. What is the cost per million output tokens, in dollars?
With softmax and cross-entropy, what is the gradient on each logit?

options.A: −ln p for every token
options.B: p − 1 for the correct token, and p for every other token
options.C: The same value for every token
options.D: 1 for the correct token, 0 for all others

prompt: An H100 does about 989 trillion operations per second and reads about 3.35 trillion bytes per second. How many operations can it do per byte read before memory stops being the bottleneck?
A 70B model's weights at 8-bit (1 byte each). How many GB?
The DPO loss is −ln σ(gap). What is the “gap”?

options.A: The number of tokens the two answers differ by
options.B: The reward model's score difference
options.C: How much more the model now favors the chosen answer over the rejected one, compared with the starting model
options.D: The difference in length between the two answers

prompt: Pre-training on one 1,000-token document. How many next-token training examples does it give?

How is the causal mask applied in code?

options.A: Add −∞ to the scores above the diagonal before softmax, so future positions get exactly 0 weight
options.B: Multiply the values of future tokens by 0.5
options.C: Delete the future tokens from the input
options.D: Set the attention weights to 0 after the weighted average

prompt: Same setup ($8 per hour, 1,000 tokens/s while busy), but the GPUs are busy only half the time. Cost per million output tokens, in dollars?
Quantization speeds up decode a lot but prefill much less. Why?

options.A: Decode is memory-bound, so fewer bytes per weight means a faster tick; prefill is compute-bound, so it gains only if the GPU also does the math in lower precision
options.B: Prefill doesn't use the weights
options.C: Prefill is already cached
options.D: Quantization only applies to output tokens

prompt: Quantizing weights to 8-bit gives decode “two multiplying wins”. What are they?

options.A: Lower temperature and less sampling
options.B: Fewer layers and a smaller vocabulary
options.C: Each tick reads half the weight bytes, and the freed memory holds more KV caches, so the batch grows
options.D: Shorter prompts and shorter answers

prompt: What does a chat template do?

options.A: Adds a second model that handles conversation
options.B: Translates the prompt into a fixed format of questions
options.C: Stores past conversations on the server
options.D: Wraps each turn in special tokens (like <|user|>, <|assistant|>) and flattens the messages list into one token string the model continues

prompt: Base model vs chat model after supervised fine-tuning (SFT): what changes?

options.A: A new answer-generation layer is added
options.B: The loss function is replaced by a reward
options.C: Only the weight values, through more training with the same next-token loss on curated prompt → answer pairs; architecture, tokenizer and loss stay the same

prompt: RLHF vs DPO: what does each need?

options.A: RLHF: a trained reward model plus reinforcement learning with generation during training. DPO: one loss directly on chosen/rejected pairs, ordinary supervised training
options.B: RLHF trains on single answers; DPO needs a full conversation
options.C: Both need a reward model; DPO just trains it faster
options.D: RLHF: only human-written answers. DPO: a reward model

options.A: Adding GPUs (tensor parallelism): more bandwidth per tick and more room for caches

options.C: Quantizing to 8-bit
